# Introduction

This file runs an exploratory K-means cluster analysis on recreational fishers in the 2025 SELTMP data. Editing `selected_vars` allows the testing of different survey response columns for the analysis. The code compares solutions with 3, 4, and 5 clusters using average silhouette width, then exports respondent assignments, cluster profiles, and selection metrics.

K-means works with numeric data and is sensitive to variable choice, missing data, and scaling. All results are exploratory, resulting clusters are not necessarily meaningful or significant.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# R Setup & housekeeping
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
	echo = TRUE,
	include = TRUE,
	message = FALSE,
	warning = FALSE)

rm(list=ls())
objects()
```

```{r}
# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(here)
```

# 1. Prepare data

```{r}
# Import Data
data_file <- readxl::read_xlsx(
  "C:/FILES/CSIRO_Internship/Rec_Fishing_Project/Data/SELTMP-2025-GBR-surveydataset_v1-0_RecFishingCLUSTERS_RyanW-Nov-3-2026.xlsx")
# Choose variables based on their response-column names from the Raw_Data sheet.
selected_vars <- c("age", "trust_science", "trust_GBRMPA")

# Set the number of clusters to compare.
k_candidates <- 3:5

# Set a random seed so results can be reproduced.
set.seed(2026)
```

```{r}
# Import specific excel sheets
data_path <- "C:/FILES/CSIRO_Internship/Rec_Fishing_Project/Data/SELTMP-2025-GBR-surveydataset_v1-0_RecFishingCLUSTERS_RyanW-Nov-3-2026.xlsx"
raw_data <- readxl::read_excel(data_path, sheet = "Raw_Data")
var_info <- readxl::read_excel(data_path, sheet = "Variable Information")

# Filter for only recreational fishers and add a row number to identify each source record.
fisher_data <- raw_data |>
  filter(Are_you_a_Rec_Fisher == 1) |>
  mutate(source_row = row_number())

# Convert all selected variables to numbers;(non-numeric entries become missing).
cluster_data <- fisher_data |>
  select(source_row, all_of(selected_vars)) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(selected_vars),
                ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(.x)))))

# Keep columns with at least one valid value and more than one distinct response.
usable_vars <- selected_vars[
  vapply(cluster_data[selected_vars],
         function(x) any(!is.na(x)) && n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE) > 1,
         logical(1))
]

# Stop if fewer than two usable response columns remain.
if (length(usable_vars) < 2) {
  stop("Select at least two columns with numeric, non-missing, varying responses.")
}

# Keep the respondent identifier and usable response columns.
cluster_data <- cluster_data |>
  select(source_row, all_of(usable_vars))

# Fill missing responses with the column median to retain respondents.
cluster_data <- cluster_data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(usable_vars),
                ~ replace(.x, is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE))))

# Standardize the responses so columns with larger scales do not dominate.
x_scaled <- scale(cluster_data |> select(all_of(usable_vars)))

# Report the number of respondents and variables used.
tibble(
  respondents = nrow(x_scaled),
  variables = ncol(x_scaled),
  selected_variables = paste(usable_vars, collapse = ", ")
)
```

# 2. Compare cluster solutions

```{r}
# Keep only cluster counts that are possible for the available respondents.
k_candidates <- k_candidates[k_candidates >= 2 & k_candidates < nrow(x_scaled)]

# Stop if none of the requested cluster counts can be tested.
if (length(k_candidates) == 0) {
  stop("There are too few respondents to fit the requested cluster counts.")
}

# Fit each candidate solution and calculate its average silhouette width.
cluster_fits <- lapply(k_candidates, function(k) {
  fit <- kmeans(x_scaled, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
  sil <- cluster::silhouette(fit$cluster, dist(x_scaled))

  list(
    k = k,
    fit = fit,
    avg_silhouette = mean(sil[, "sil_width"])
  )
})

# Summarize the separation and within-cluster variation for each solution.
selection_metrics <- tibble(
  clusters = vapply(cluster_fits, function(x) x$k, integer(1)),
  average_silhouette = vapply(cluster_fits, function(x) x$avg_silhouette, numeric(1)),
  total_withinss = vapply(cluster_fits, function(x) x$fit$tot.withinss, numeric(1))
) |>
  arrange(desc(average_silhouette))

# Select the candidate with the highest average silhouette width.
best_k <- selection_metrics$clusters[[1]]
best_fit <- cluster_fits[[which(k_candidates == best_k)]]$fit

# Display the comparison and selected number of clusters.
selection_metrics

# Note: 
# average silhouette ranges from -1 to 1 with positive values indicating data points are far away from each cluster
# values near zero indicate they are on the boarder between clusters and 
# negative values indicate they are closer to a neighboring cluster than their own

# Large drops in the value of total withinss as you add more clusters suggest you have found a distinct cluster 
# Diminishing returns (small drops) as you add more clusters suggest they may be arbitrary rather than distinct

```

# 3. Describe and export clusters

```{r}
# Add each respondent's assigned cluster to the selected response data.
cluster_assignments <- cluster_data |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(best_fit$cluster))

# Calculate each cluster's size and mean responses on the original scales.
cluster_profiles <- cluster_assignments |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    respondents = n(),
    across(all_of(usable_vars), mean),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(percent_of_sample = respondents / sum(respondents) * 100)

# Match selected columns to their labels in the variable dictionary.
variable_key <- tibble(variable = usable_vars) |>
  left_join(
    var_info |> select(variable = `Variable short name`, label = Label),
    by = "variable"
  )

# Show cluster sizes, percentages, and mean responses.
cluster_profiles
```
